..
Issued at 1130 AM CST Mon Nov 2 2026

Midday satellite imagery clearly defined a strong closed
midlevel cyclone over northeast New Mexico. The associated dry
slot has temporarily cleared the sky over SW KS, with stratus
lingering over eastern zones. Mesoanalysis outlined an axis of
moderate instability, with CAPE in excess of 1000 J/kg, across
the eastern zones, colocated with bulk shear of 30-40 kts. 
This environment will support supercell structures upon
initiation across the southeast zones 3-6 pm. Hail of 1-2 inches
in diameter and wind gusts of 50-70 mph are possible from the
strongest storms. Given favorable low level shear/SRH and low
LCL heights, a tornado risk is apparent. Much of this threat
should manifest east of the DDC CWA, but can't rule out
tornadoes across the southeast zones for 1-2 hours before
sunset. Simultaneously, a strong deformation zone of moderate to
heavy rain will blossom across the western/northwest zones this
afternoon/evening, in response to 560 dm cyclone ejecting into
the southeast zones by midnight. After about sunset, the
associated intense cold front will race through SW KS, reaching
the central zones about 6 pm, and exiting the southeast zones
about 3 am, behind the departing surface/midlevel cyclones.
Intense northwest winds are expected tonight through Tuesday
morning. NBM guidance has increased some, but is still several 
knots lower than the strongest guidance. Gusts over 50 mph will
be common tonight through Tuesday midday, with the strongest 
winds tied to the preferred US 83 corridor. Most models show
850 mb winds flirting with about 50 kts (58 mph) at about 2k 
ft, enough to support high wind warning criteria gusts, given 
sufficient mixing through the nocturnal boundary layer. A short 
fuse high wind warning may still be issued; it is marginal, but 
models are notorious for underestimating deformation winds in 
departing cyclones in SW KS. 

Widespread soaking rain is expected tonight through Tuesday
morning in the deformation zone, across western to northwest
zones. Rainfall amounts of 1/2 to 1 inch will be common in 
these zones, with 12z NAM suggesting amounts in excess of 
2 inches where the deformation zone can pivot in place the 
longest (roughly Garden City to Hays). NBM has correctly 
trended pops up into the definite category (90-100%) across 
these zones. After sunset, most instability is expected to be 
eliminated, as such there is very little thunder in the forecast
tonight through Tuesday morning.

Tuesday will remind us that it is November, with strong
northwest winds and dramatically cooler temperatures. Models
reduce 850 temperatures to the +4-6C range, and along with
lingering stratus through midday, temperatures will struggle
into the 50s. NBM continues to correctly trend downward through
the mid 50s Tuesday. Winds will diminish through the day, but
wind chill indices will be near 30 Tuesday morning. 

Strong radiational cooling is forecast Tuesday night through
sunrise Wednesday, with light winds, a clear sky and a much more
seasonably colder air mass. Expect 30s to be common sunrise
Wednesday, which sounds cold, but is perfectly normal for early
November. Air does not look sufficiently cold for a killing
freeze, although some patchy frost is probable northwest zones. 

A passing weak shortwave should generate some limited scattered
showers late Wednesday/early Thursday. This system will be
moisture starved with no impacts and QPF limited. 

Friday through Sunday, the synoptic pattern returns to a quiet
dry regime, with troughing deepening over the Great Lakes and
ridging over the Desert Southwest. The resulting northwest flow
will force gulf moisture away from SW KS, with highest
confidence of a dry forecast through next weekend.
